source: FindMyPast — Hampshire Baptisms and Marriages (Hampshire Genealogical Society); England Births & Baptisms and England Marriages 1538–1975; National Burial Index (Gloucestershire FHS)

marriage.line: ROBERT DARCY married JEAN WARD at PORTSEA ST MARY on 21 JUNE 1779
marriage.means: This archive has carried Robert D'Arcy's marriage on a family tree for its entire existence, with no record behind it. Here it is. Nine months later, on 19 March 1780, the same church baptised their son Joseph.

darcy.baptism: Joseph D'Arcy, baptised Portsea St Mary 19 March 1780, SON, father ROBERT, mother JEAN — the Hampshire Genealogical Society's own transcription, independent of the FreeREG entry this archive has been quoting.

coverage.test: John Smith at Portsea, 1770–1794, in FindMyPast's Hampshire collections.
coverage.result: Portsea St Mary baptisms come back for 1770, 1771, 1772, 1774, 1775, 1779, 1782 (twice), 1785, 1786, 1788 (twice), 1789, 1790, 1791 and 1792 — continuous across the whole window, where FreeREG holds twenty-two months.
coverage.verdict: So the silence around Joseph is now real. Searching the same window for every D'Arcy spelling returns HIM AND NOBODY ELSE. Robert and Jean baptised one child at Portsea St Mary, not a family.
coverage.careful: Which is not the same as saying they had one child. A regiment moves. The couple married at Portsea in 1779, baptised Joseph there in 1780, and by 1806 a daughter was marrying at Chatham — the children in between will be in garrison parishes this search has not touched.

saniger.note: The archive has said for months that five of the tree's six Saniger generations could not be tested because FreeREG's Berkeley transcript stops in 1677. Every one of the following is a Berkeley record from after 1677.
rows: The tree gives 23 August 1744 at Berkeley. The same day.
A name this archive has never had. John was baptised five weeks later.
The tree gives John's birth as 15 May 1769. Baptised three days later.
Born about 1744. The tree says he died about 1819.
Born about 1769. The tree says he died on 10 March 1824 — ten months out.
saniger.gap: Hannah's own baptism is not in the index. Her father's children appear at Berkeley in 1801, 1803 and 1808, and the tree puts her birth on 23 July 1805 — exactly in the space between. That is a gap in a transcription, not an absence in a register: FamilySearch's England Births & Baptisms is not a complete copy of Berkeley St Mary, and the original book is what will settle it.
saniger.verdict: Four generations of the tree — Thomas of 1711, Thomas of 1744, John of 1769, Hannah of 1805 — now stand on parish records rather than on somebody's assertion. The chain the archive called untestable was testable the whole time.

wrongTree: John Saniger died 10 March 1824 at Berkeley
Buried at Berkeley St Mary the Virgin on 16 JANUARY 1825, aged 55. The tree is ten months early.
Hannah Saniger was born at Berkeley on 23 July 1805
Not yet found, but her father's other children are baptised there in 1801, 1803 and 1808, and the 1851 census gives her birthplace as Berkeley.

audit.head: Every marriage this archive cites, re-opened
audit.lede: On 16 September a claim carried by every online tree — that John Saniger married Lydia Jones at Berkeley in 1797 — was disproved by opening a transcript and reading one field the result row does not show: **the spouse's surname**. The man was a Sawyer. That raised an obvious question about this archive's own work, and it has now been answered rather than assumed.
audit.how: **All 51 marriage entries in the register.** Most were never at risk: FreeREG publishes a full register transcript with both parties named, the Queensland index gives a registration number that carries both, and a newspaper notice prints the names in full. **Five came from FindMyPast index sets, where the result row is the trap.** **All five have now been re-opened at transcript level — four on 17 September, the fifth on the 20th — and all five hold.**
rows: Robert Darcy m. Jean Ward · Portsea St Mary, 21 June 1779
Hannah Saniger m. James Wakefield · Bristol, 17 October 1831
Thomas Saniger m. Catherine Cotton · Berkeley, 10 April 1769
Thomas Sanigre m. Martha Golding · Bristol, 24 August 1828
Joseph Ward m. Marth Gairden · South Leith, 27 October 1747
GAIRDEN — confirmed, and her father with her
audit.oneHead: And the fifth, closed three days later
audit.one: **Joseph Ward and Marth Gairden, South Leith, 27 October 1747** could not be re-opened on 17 September because the record set would not resolve under any `datasetname` tried. It resolves through a **cross-set search with a place** instead — `place=south+leith` and no dataset at all. The transcript confirms **GAIRDEN**, and carries a field the result row never shows: **Spouse's father — WILLIAM GAIRDEN.** The argument made for it on the 17th, that a result row has never carried a father so somebody must have read past the row, turns out to have been right. It is now checked rather than argued. **All five hold.**
audit.defectHead: The defect is FindMyPast's, and it is not one dataset's quirk
audit.defect: The Portsea marriage was the useful test, because **Hampshire Marriages is a different collection with a different owner** — the Hampshire Genealogical Society — and its result row has exactly the same columns: *First name · Last name · Marriage year · **Spouse's first name(s)** · Place*. No surname. So a reader who searches a bride by her forename, matches a groom's forename, a year and a parish, and stops at the results page, will build a false marriage on any FindMyPast set they use. **That is how «Lydia Jones» got into every tree on the internet**, and the only defence is the extra click.
audit.smallHead: And one small thing worth knowing
audit.small: The founding marriage of this whole line is indexed under **DARCY**, not D'Arcy. The archive's alias list already carries both, which is the only reason the search found it at all.

instrument.head: Ways this site returns a number that is not about the world
instrument.lede: A null is only a fact about the world if the search could have found the thing it did not find — and a total is only a fact about the world if the thing it counts is the thing it is called. Over **20 and 21 September** this archive caught FindMyPast doing both wrong, in the ways listed below, **each of which had already been published here as a finding or was about to be.** They are written down together because the next session will meet them again.
rows: **CATHERINE SMITH born about 1789 in Sussex returns nothing** in the 1861 census, which cannot be true of any English county. The combination silently returns zero on the census sets. Three searches for the Brighton sisters had been built on it.

Asking for SMITH in **1790** returns twenty rows dated 1673, 1678, 1689, 1690, 1692, 1693, 1704, 1707, 1709, 1781, 1802, 1803 and 1826 — **and no 1790 at all**. The parameter is thrown away and the search answers a different question.
A page read a moment too early

The identical query for **COTTON baptisms in Gloucestershire** returns **nothing** sorted ascending and a page of results sorted descending. Results render asynchronously, so a zero read too soon is **indistinguishable from a real zero** — and nothing on the page says which it was.
`yearofbaptism` against an entry indexed by birth

**England Births & Baptisms holds two kinds of entry** — some with a baptism year, some with only a birth year — and the filters are not interchangeable. DARCY unfiltered returns rows dated 1666, 1707 and 1708 whose **«Baptism year» column is empty**, so every `yearofbaptism` search against that surname returns nothing whatever the years.
An exact-spelling search is exactly exact

**SANIGRE returns Thomas Sinegar's 1828 marriage and nothing else in England returns it.** SANIGER asked the same way in the same county and window returns 8 marriages, SANIGAR returns 3, and **he is in neither.** The surname box answers for a string, not for a name — so a null recorded as «not found in any spelling» is only ever as wide as the list of spellings somebody typed, and the list here came from a baptism index in which this form does not occur at all.
The result count counts rows, not events

**298 index entries across the five commonest spellings of this surname are 246 baptisms.** The set transcribes registers and bishops' transcripts and some parishes twice over: Mary, daughter of Samuell, is indexed **four times** at Berkeley in 1688, and Sarah, daughter of William, four times at Bristol in 1839. The duplication is not even — SANIGER and SANIGAR hold 48 of the 50 repeats and SINNEGAR holds none — so an entry count measures how often a parish was typed up as much as how often a name was written.
Two plausible parameter names that quietly mean nothing

The GRO death index prints a **District** column and is addressed by `district`. Give it `place` or `registrationdistrict` instead — both perfectly reasonable names, one of them the column's own full title — and it returns **nought** with no complaint. **SMITH at `place=lymington` returns zero**, which cannot be true of any English district; `district=reading` narrows 128 Joseph Smiths of 1848 down to the right one. Nothing on the page distinguishes a parameter it ignored from a record that is not there.
A filter on a column that is mostly empty

«Newspapers & Publications» here is a **name index to BMD notices**, not the British Newspaper Archive's full text, and its Year column is blank for most rows. **SMITH returns 674,001 notices unfiltered and 0 with a year of death of 1827 ± 2.** The filter is working exactly as asked and discarding everything that was never dated. Forename filtering does work — Robert D'Arcy narrows 4,459 rows to 42 — so nothing on the page suggests the year is the problem.
A give-or-take that silently becomes an exact year

`yearofbaptism_offset` accepts any integer, not only the seven in the dropdown — **SANIGER baptised 1792 returns 5 at offset 0, 7 at offset 3 and 58 at offset 40.** Above 40 it does not widen, and it does not complain: **offset 45 returns 5, which is exactly the offset-0 count.** The widest search a reader can ask for silently becomes the narrowest one there is. **This is the worst of the faults on this page**, because every other one hands back a zero and a zero at least looks like an answer worth checking. This hands back a real, small, plausible result with nothing wrong with its face. Measured here on 21 September after the Defranceski session found it on an Italian surname and corrected its own first account of it.
every null with a wide window
instrument.rule:
This archive already required every null to name a control. That is not enough for a site read through a browser. **A control has to be run in the same session, through the same query shape, and return something — not merely exist as a principle.** A null with a control that was itself a zero is not a control; it is two zeros and a hope. Every FindMyPast null recorded here on 20 September carries a control that returned rows.

**And on 21 September the rule gained a method, not just a warning.** The surname box takes **wildcards**. `S*N*G*` asked of Gloucestershire marriages for 1827-1829 returns 53 rows, and among them is **Thomas Sanigre, 1828** — the marriage eight named spellings had failed to find and this archive had recorded as absent — together with **one marriage indexed as both SANIGER and SANIGOR** at Rodborough in 1827. A list of spellings is a guess about a clerk; a wildcard is not. The cost is strangers — the same 53 rows hold Sanger, Shearing and Sheering — so **the trade is a wider net inside a narrow window, read row by row**, rather than a narrow net cast across a century. Where a question has a place and a decade, that is now the first search and the spelling list is the second.

**And the same day showed what «the same query shape» does not cover.** This archive published «None, in any spelling» for Sanigers at Chew Magna with a control beside it, and the parish register holds two — Charles Sinagar 1816 and William Sinegar 1822, children of Simon and Elizabeth. The control was a search at **Berkeley**. It returned 252 rows, so it proved the site was answering; it could not prove that the **Chew Magna** page had finished rendering, which is the one thing that had to be true. **A control that changes the field under test is not testing that field.** Where a query takes a wildcard, the wildcard is the better control: it re-asks the same field in a way that cannot fail for the reason a spelling list fails. `S*N*G*R` at Chew Magna returns four records and two of them are the name. **check_controls.py now refuses a new FindMyPast null that claims «any spelling» without one.**

**One line added to that on the evening of the 21st, from the Defranceski session, and it is the operational half.** A wildcard buys reach by giving up discrimination, and **it does not report which of the two it is currently doing**. So make it report: **run the exact spelling first and read the ratio against the wildcard.** One in twenty here; one in a hundred and twenty for a surname whose stem is native English. That single extra query is the difference between a tool that saves a day and one that invents a family, and it is cheaper than either.
instrument.costHead: What it cost, and the one thing that cannot go wrong
instrument.cost:
**Three findings were withdrawn before publication and one after.** The sisters' 1861 absence was reclassified from «null» to «blocked — the question was never asked». Robert's Army List gap is now stated as possibly the publisher's rather than the man's. **Catherine Cotton's origins were published as «inconclusive» and then, an hour later, re-run and published as a proper controlled null** — 27 Cotton baptisms in the county in the right eleven years and no Catherine among them. That is the sequence this rule is meant to produce: doubt the instrument, re-run it, and let the finding stand only when a control comes back with something.

**21 September added two more, and both had already been published.** The spelling table's headline said «371 baptisms» where it had counted 371 index entries, on two pages. And a null saying Thomas Sinegar's marriage was «not found, in any spelling» had stood on /searched for eight days while /thomas-sinegar carried the marriage itself. **Own errors 38 and 39.**

**One piece of good news, and it is structural.** A `datasetname` that names no real set returns a **500 error**, not a zero — proved by asking for a non-conformist set that does not exist beside one that does. So a zero from this site is always a zero from a set that is really there. It does nothing about the faults above, where the set is real and the filter is the liar, but it closes off a whole class of false null that a mistyped set name would otherwise create silently.
